name: Design a Ride-Sharing Service
intent: Match riders with nearby drivers within seconds, keep a map of moving cars up to date, and run each trip from request to payment without double-booking anyone.
codeTitle: finding the nearest driver with a grid index
finalIntro: One ride from a driver's location update to the final payment.
prompt: Design a service like Uber or Lyft. Riders request a ride from where they stand, the nearest suitable driver is offered the trip, and both of them watch each other move on a map until the ride ends and the rider is charged.
functional: Drivers go online and report their location continuously
A rider requests a ride and is matched with a nearby available driver
A driver can accept or decline an offer
Rider and driver see each other's position live during pickup and the trip
Charge the rider once when the trip finishes
Optional: show an estimated price that rises when demand is high
nonFunctional: Matching takes a few seconds at most
One driver is never given two trips at the same time, and one rider never gets two cars
Location writes are constant and enormous: every online driver reports every few seconds
A slightly stale driver location is fine, but a lost trip or a double charge is not
Stay up during busy periods such as a stadium emptying or a rainy rush hour
Work on weak mobile connections that drop and reconnect

firstAttempt.text: One web server and one database. A drivers table holds each driver's latest latitude, longitude and status. Drivers send their position every few seconds and the server updates their row. A ride request loads the available drivers, computes the distance to each one, and offers the trip to the closest. It works for a small town.
limits: Finding the nearest driver means measuring the distance to every driver, so each request gets slower as the fleet grows
Thousands of location updates per second hammer the same table that matching and trips depend on
Two requests at the same moment can both pick the same free driver
Riders and drivers have to keep asking the server for new positions, which is slow and wastes battery
One machine and one database is the only way in, so any failure stops every ride

steps.title: Index drivers by map cell, in memory
steps.problem: Measuring the distance to every driver for every request gets slower with every driver added, and the question is only ever about the few cars nearby.
steps.fix: Split the map into a grid of cells and keep each driver's latest position in an in-memory index under their cell. To find drivers near a rider, look in the rider's cell and then the rings of cells around it, widening only until no unvisited cell could hold a closer car. Production systems use geohashes or hexagonal cells for the same idea. Trips stay in a normal database, and the API sits in front of both.
steps.tradeoff: A search touches a handful of cells, however big the fleet is. A driver changes cells as they move, so every update may need to move them, and a car just across a cell border is missed if you only look in the rider's own cell.

steps.title: Shard the index by area and keep the trail on a stream
steps.problem: Every online driver writes a new position every few seconds, which is far more than one machine handles, and storing every point in the main database would drown it.
steps.fix: Shard the location index by geographic area, so each shard owns a set of cells, for example by hashing the cell id. A location update overwrites the driver's single latest entry, which is cheap and needs no disk. The same update is also appended to a stream, and a consumer writes the trail into cheap storage for trip history, billing disputes and analytics.
steps.tradeoff: Writes spread over many machines and the live index stays small, because it only holds the latest position. Searches near a shard boundary must ask two shards, and a busy downtown area can overload its shard unless it is split into smaller cells.

steps.title: Match with an atomic claim and a timeout
steps.problem: Two riders can pick the same driver in the same instant, and a driver who never answers an offer holds up the rider for as long as it takes.
steps.fix: A matching service finds the nearest candidates in the index and tries them one at a time. Before offering a trip it claims the driver with one atomic compare-and-set: free becomes offered for this trip, and the claim fails if anyone else got there first. The offer carries a 10 to 15 second timeout. A decline or a timeout releases the claim, and the service moves to the next candidate.
steps.tradeoff: A driver can never hold two trips, and a rider is never stuck on a silent phone. Matching one rider at a time can pick a worse overall pairing than looking at everyone waiting in the same moment, so busy cities also match in small batches.

steps.title: Push offers and positions over persistent connections
steps.problem: Phones that keep asking the server where the car is waste battery and show the position late, and a driver cannot be offered a trip unless the server can reach them.
steps.fix: Every app keeps a WebSocket open to a push gateway. Offers, driver positions and trip updates travel down that connection the moment they happen. The gateway servers are stateless about trips: they know which connection belongs to which user and nothing else, and the apps reconnect and ask for the current trip state after any break.
steps.tradeoff: Updates arrive within a second or two and battery use drops, because the app is not polling. The gateway holds many open connections, so it is scaled and drained carefully, and a dropped connection must never lose an offer, so offers are also kept as trip state.

steps.title: Run the trip as a state machine and charge exactly once
steps.problem: A trip has many steps, such as requested, matched, picked up, completed and paid, and a crash or a retry between steps must not lose a trip or charge a rider twice.
steps.fix: Each trip is a row with a state and only allowed moves, for example matched to picked up but never completed to requested. Each move is a conditional update, so repeated or late messages do nothing. When a trip completes, the trip service records the fare and publishes a payment request carrying a key built from the trip id, so the payment service charges once however many times the request arrives.
steps.tradeoff: Trips survive crashes and duplicates, and every state change leaves an audit trail. Payment happens just after the trip rather than inside the same transaction, so there is a short window where a trip is complete and not yet paid, which a retry process and a reconciliation job close.

steps.title: Count demand per area to price surges
steps.problem: When riders far outnumber drivers in one area, matching slows and waits grow, and the system needs a way to bring more drivers in and slow down demand.
steps.fix: A counter service reads the same location and request streams and keeps, for each cell, the number of waiting riders and free drivers over the last minute or two. A price multiplier is derived from that ratio, smoothed so it does not jump, and the API quotes it to riders before they confirm. The price they were quoted is locked into the trip.
steps.tradeoff: Price follows real conditions and pulls drivers toward busy areas. The numbers lag by a little, the multiplier needs a cap and clear messages to stay fair and trusted, and a quoted price must never change after the rider confirms.

failures.impact: Drivers in its area vanish from the map, and riders there get no matches.
failures.answer: The index only holds the latest positions, and drivers send a new one every few seconds, so a replacement shard (or a replica promoted to take over) is full again within a few seconds of the first updates. Meanwhile the matching service widens its search to neighbouring shards, and the trail kept on the stream is not affected.

failures.scenario: The matching service crashes in the middle of an offer
failures.impact: A driver is claimed for a trip that nobody is managing, so the rider waits and the driver is stuck.
failures.answer: A claim carries an expiry, so an orphaned claim releases itself after the offer timeout. Trips stay in the database in a requested state, and another matching worker picks up any request that has been waiting too long. Because claims and state changes are conditional, a second worker cannot create a double booking.

failures.scenario: A stadium empties and thousands of riders request cars within two minutes
failures.impact: Requests far outnumber nearby drivers, matching searches pile up, and the cells around the stadium get overloaded.
failures.answer: Requests are queued per area and matched in order, with a cap on waiting time before riders are told the real wait. Surge pricing draws drivers toward the area and thins out demand, the index shards for that area can be split further, and rate limits stop one client from sending repeated requests.

failures.scenario: The payment provider is down when a trip ends
failures.impact: The rider has arrived, and the charge cannot be made.
failures.answer: The trip is completed regardless and the payment request is kept safe in the outbox. The payment service retries with backoff using the same trip-based key, so the charge is made once when the provider returns. The rider is told the receipt will follow, and a daily reconciliation catches anything missed.

alternatives.title: How to index locations

options.name: Latitude and longitude columns in a SQL table
options.pro: Nothing new to learn, and fine for a small fleet
options.con: Nearby searches scan lots of rows, and constant updates compete with trip data

options.name: Geohash or hexagonal cells in an in-memory store
options.pro: A search reads a few cells, and updates are cheap overwrites
options.con: Cell borders need neighbour lookups, and the size of a cell is a choice that must be tuned

options.name: A quadtree that splits busy areas
options.pro: Dense areas get small cells and empty areas stay large
options.con: More complicated to build, shard and rebalance as drivers move

alternatives.pick: Fixed cells (geohash or hexagons) in memory, with smaller cells for busy cities. It is simple, and easy to shard.

alternatives.title: How to choose the driver

options.name: Nearest driver first
options.pro: Simple, fast, and easy to explain
options.con: Straight-line distance can differ a lot from driving time across rivers and one-way streets

options.name: Best estimated arrival time
options.pro: Better for riders, because it uses road distance and traffic
options.con: Needs a routing service, and an estimate for every candidate costs time

options.name: Batch and match everyone waiting together
options.pro: Better overall pairing and shorter total waiting in busy areas
options.con: Every rider waits a few extra seconds for the batch to close

alternatives.pick: Rank a short list of nearby drivers by estimated arrival time, and match in small batches when demand is high.

alternatives.title: How the apps get updates

options.name: Polling every few seconds
options.pro: Works everywhere and needs no special servers
options.con: Wasteful, and positions are always a few seconds out of date

options.name: WebSocket connection per app
options.pro: Instant two-way updates and the lowest battery use
options.con: Many open connections to manage, and every reconnect needs the current state

options.name: Mobile push notifications
options.pro: Reaches an app that is closed
options.con: Delivery is not guaranteed or instant, so it is only a wake-up for the offer, not a live feed

alternatives.pick: WebSockets while the app is open, with a push notification to wake a driver's app when an offer arrives.

alternatives.title: Who records a trip's state

options.name: One row per trip with conditional updates
options.pro: Simple and fast to read, and easy to keep consistent
options.con: History of how it got to this state is only as good as the log you add

options.name: An event log per trip (event sourcing)
options.pro: A complete audit trail, and states can be rebuilt
options.con: More machinery, and reading the current state needs a projection

alternatives.pick: A row with conditional updates and a small history table. Move to an event log only when audits or disputes make the full history essential.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The API and the push gateway.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The location index, the trail and the trip database.

quiz.question: A city has 100,000 online drivers. Each ride request loads every free driver, computes the distance to each one and offers the trip to the closest. At 50 requests per second the CPU is saturated, and matching gets slower every time the fleet grows. What is the best fix?
options: Add separate indexes on the latitude and longitude columns so the database can range-scan both columns and intersect the results
Add read replicas of the drivers table and spread the distance calculations for each ride request across those replicas
Index drivers in memory by map cell id and search the rider's cell and the rings of cells around it
Cache the nearest driver per rider for 30 seconds
quiz.explanation: A grid index makes a search touch a handful of cells, whatever the fleet size. Two single-column indexes still return a huge strip of the map for each range, so most rows are still scanned. Replicas only spread the same full scan over more machines.

quiz.question: Assume 500,000 drivers are online and each reports a position every 4 seconds, and one in-memory index node handles about 25,000 updates per second. Trip history must still be kept for billing disputes. Which design fits?
options: Shard the index by map area over at least 6 nodes, overwrite each driver's single latest entry, and also append every update to a stream for the trail
Use one index node with a disk write-ahead log for every update, since location data must be durable
Write the updates to the trips database in batches of 1,000, because that database already stores the trail
Ask drivers to report every 20 seconds so that one node stays under its limit, even though cars move about 250 m between updates
quiz.explanation: 500,000 / 4 s is 125,000 updates per second, five times one node's limit, so the index must be sharded, with headroom. Overwriting the latest position is cheap, and the stream keeps the history away from the live index. Slower reporting hits the limit with no headroom and makes matching use positions hundreds of metres old.

quiz.question: Matching worker W1 claims driver D for rider R1 with an atomic compare-and-set and sends the offer, which times out after 15 seconds. W1 then crashes. Meanwhile the matching worker for rider R2 finds D as its closest candidate. What should happen?
options: R2's worker takes D immediately, because the worker that made the claim has crashed and can no longer complete its offer to the driver
The claim stays in place until W1 reports the offer finished, so a crashed worker can never cause a double booking of the driver
Every ride request goes to two matching workers at the same time, so the crash of one worker is always covered by the other
R2's claim fails and R2 tries the next candidate. The claim expires by itself, and another worker re-picks R1's request
quiz.explanation: The claim carries an expiry, so an orphaned claim frees itself and the conditional update stops anyone else taking D before then. Taking D at once is risky, because D's phone may still be showing R1's offer and could accept it. A claim that never expires would leave D stuck for ever.
